result.summary: Telemachus returns to the palace, greets Penelope and reports what he learned at Pylos and Sparta. Ulysses, disguised as a beggar, goes to town with Eumaeus, is abused by Melanthius, is recognised only by his dying dog Argos, and is struck by Antinous with a footstool. Penelope asks to see the beggar, and he puts her off until evening.

scenes.title: Telemachus leaves the farm
scenes.summary: Telemachus tells Eumaeus to bring the stranger to town and goes ahead. Ulysses agrees to follow once he has warmed himself.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses must keep his disguise and bear the cold and the dismissive talk.

scenes.title: Reunion with Penelope
scenes.summary: Telemachus is greeted by Euryclea and Penelope, sends his mother to pray, and meets his father's friends. He settles Piraeus and Theoclymenus in his house.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus faces the suitors' hidden malice while hoping for revenge.

scenes.title: Telemachus reports his journey
scenes.summary: Telemachus tells Penelope of Nestor, Menelaus and Calypso's captive Ulysses. Theoclymenus prophesies that Ulysses is already in Ithaca. The suitors go in to their dinner.
scenes.stakes: Penelope's hope of her husband's return hangs on the reports.

scenes.title: Melanthius insults Ulysses
scenes.summary: Ulysses and Eumaeus reach the fountain, where Melanthius abuses and kicks Ulysses. Ulysses holds back his anger.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks exposing himself if he strikes back.

scenes.title: The dog Argos
scenes.summary: Ulysses admires his house, then sees his old hound Argos. The dog recognises him and dies.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses cannot show grief without betraying himself.

scenes.title: Antinous strikes the beggar
scenes.summary: Ulysses begs among the suitors and tells a false tale of Egypt. Antinous throws a footstool at him and Telemachus seethes.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses faces violence and could be exposed.

scenes.title: Penelope summons the beggar
scenes.summary: Penelope curses Antinous and sends for the stranger. Ulysses asks to wait until sundown. Eumaeus returns to his pigs.
scenes.stakes: Penelope longs for news of her husband while the suitors threaten.

characters.name: Minerva
characters.description: Protects Ulysses and prompts him to beg

characters.name: Menelaus
characters.description: King of Lacedaemon, quoted by Telemachus

notable_quotes.reason: Argos wags his tail at his disguised master, the poignant recognition.
Argos dies the moment he recognises Ulysses.
A suitor warns that gods roam disguised to judge men's conduct.

analysis.text: Hospitality and its abuse: the suitors mistreat a beggar, who may be a god, and Antinous marks himself for punishment.
Loyalty is shown by the dog and the servants, while disguise lets Ulysses test who is faithful.

legacy.text: The death of Argos is among literature's best-known scenes of animal loyalty and has been echoed by many later writers.

fun_facts.text: Argos is the earliest dog in Western literature to be named and given such a portrait.

language_notes.text: "Child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" is a stock Homeric formula for daybreak, repeated throughout the poem.
"Had a warm" means got warm; Ulysses asks to wait until the sun has heated the day.
"Perished with cold" means nearly frozen to death, an idiom.
The "cloister" is the colonnaded porch or courtyard of the house; a "bearing-post" is a supporting pillar.
A hecatomb was a large sacrifice, originally of a hundred oxen, offered to the gods.
"Vouchsafe" means to grant graciously.
Pylos is Nestor's kingdom; Telemachus went there first to seek news of his father.
"In heaven's wisdom doomed" means the gods willed the suffering; the war was understood as divinely ordained.
A "hind" is a female deer; a "dell" is a small wooded valley.
"A short shrift and a sorry wedding" means a swift, merciless end and a grim marriage; "shrift" originally meant brief time granted before execution.
"Prevaricate" means to speak evasively or dodge the truth.
The "old man of the sea" is the sea-god Proteus, who Menelaus forced to reveal truths in Book 4.
"Discs" refers to throwing the discus, a common aristocratic pastime, here used idly by the suitors.
A "station hand" is a worker at the outlying farmstead (the "station") where Eumaeus keeps the pigs.
Ithacus, Neritus and Polyctor are legendary early figures of Ithaca; the island and its mountain are named for them, so the fountain is ancient.
Echoes the proverb "birds of a feather flock together"; the Greek says that the god leads like to like.
A man who begs "swords and cauldrons" asks for valuable gifts as a warrior would, not scraps; cauldrons were prized gifts.
"Wantonness" here means reckless, unprovoked cruelty.
Burning thigh bones wrapped in fat was the standard Greek sacrifice, so Eumaeus reminds the nymphs of Ulysses' past piety.
Battlements are a parapet with gaps along a wall's top, used for defence. The "outer court" is the walled enclosure around the house.
Ulysses says music is made by the gods to accompany feasting, reflecting the Greek view that song was a divine gift.
"Case-hardened" means toughened, like metal given a hard surface; here, made insensitive by suffering.
"Close" means an enclosed field or yard; the dung is to be carted off to fertilise it.
"Cloister" here means the covered colonnade or hall of the house, where the suitors feast.
A bearing-post is a pillar supporting the roof; 'rule and line' are the carpenter's straightedge and chalked cord for true measurement.
'From left to right' means moving around the hall in the direction a wine-server would go, so each suitor is approached in turn.
Eumaeus lists skilled wanderers (seer, healer, carpenter, bard) who were welcomed as useful, in contrast to a mere beggar.
The stool is a footstool; 'dainty feet' mocks Antinous' soft, pampered way of life.
'I will give you Egypt and Cyprus over again' means he will make the beggar suffer worse than in the tale he just told.
Refers to the Greek belief that gods wandered disguised as strangers to test human behavior, especially hospitality to guests and beggars.
"Banqueting-cloister" means the covered colonnade or porch around the hall's court, where the suitors feast.
"Nurse" is a respectful form of address to an older female servant, here Eurynome. The "147" is a stray footnote marker.
The narrator breaks in with "you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus," addressing him directly, a Homeric habit used for Eumaeus.
Minos was the legendary king of Crete; the Thesprotians were a people of northwestern Greece. Ulysses' false tale places him among them.
A sneeze was taken as a lucky omen, here confirming Penelope's words that the suitors will die.
"Lay my saying to your heart" means take what I say seriously and remember it.
"Close up to the fire": Ulysses wants the hearth seat, which suits his thin clothes and also a private evening talk.

context_notes.text: Diana (the Greek Artemis) is goddess of the hunt; Venus (Aphrodite) is goddess of love. Both are praised for beauty.
Telemachus secretly went to Pylos to seek news of his father from Nestor, without telling Penelope.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) is Telemachus' divine protector and often enhances his appearance and confidence.
The presents from Menelaus were guest-gifts, valuable treasures Telemachus received on his journey.
Lacedaemon is Sparta, the kingdom of Menelaus and Helen.
Calypso is a nymph who detained Ulysses on her island for years, wanting him as husband.
Medon is a herald-servant to the suitors; he later is spared by Ulysses for his decency.
Nymphs were minor female nature spirits tied to springs and groves. Travellers sacrificed at their altars for safe passage.
Melanthius is the goatherd of Ulysses' household, but he sides with the suitors and fawns on them.
Eurymachus is one of the leading suitors, so Melanthius gains favour by sitting near him.
Phemius is the household bard, forced to entertain the suitors who are consuming Ulysses' property.
Argos was raised by Ulysses before he left for Troy, twenty years earlier, so the dog is extremely old.
Eumaeus voices an ancient view that slavery diminishes a person; he himself was a slave, born a prince and stolen as a child.
The threshold of ash-wood is where Ulysses sits; beggars sat at the entrance, and this doorway later becomes the scene of the slaughter.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is Ulysses' divine protector; she here sets up the suitors' testing and fixes their doom.
Egypt raids were a familiar adventure in Greek tales; Ulysses invents a false identity as a ruined raider.
Apollo, god of the bow and plague, was often invoked to strike down enemies with sudden death.
Ulysses is in his own house disguised as a beggar, so Penelope does not know he is nearby.
The suitors have been consuming Ulysses' household livestock and wine while courting Penelope, a heavy burden on the estate.

literary_notes.text: Telemachus' striding off and brooding on revenge shows how he has matured into a determined, purposeful young man.
Penelope's beauty is compared to goddesses, stressing her dignity and grace even in tears.
"Fair words in their mouths and malice in their hearts" contrasts the suitors' outward courtesy with hidden hostility.
Telemachus speaks politely and casually of killing the suitors, while they are unaware of the plan against them.
Menelaus compares the suitors to a hind laying her fawns in a lion's lair, casting them as foolish prey and Ulysses as the lion.
Theoclymenus says Ulysses is already in Ithaca; the audience knows he is, disguised as a beggar, nearby.
The suitors' carefree games and old insolence hint at their blindness to the coming reckoning.
Medon's cheerful remark about dinner is ironic, since the suitors' feasting will end in their slaughter.
Ulysses is compared to a broken-down tramp, stressing how complete his disguise as a beggar is.
Melanthius mocks the beggar as lazy and greedy, though the man is the true master of the estate.
Melanthius kicks his own master without knowing it; the audience knows Ulysses will later punish him.
Ulysses' inner debate between violence and endurance shows his self-control and cunning, key to his disguise.
Hunger is called an "enemy" that drives men to sea and war, treating a bodily need as a hostile force.
Argos's small gestures, ears down and tail wagging while unable to approach, move the reader through quiet, helpless loyalty.
Ulysses secretly wipes away a tear, showing real feeling beneath his disguise and his need to stay hidden.
Eumaeus speaks of Ulysses as lost while the man himself stands beside him; the reader knows the truth.
Eumaeus's departure and Argos's death come together abruptly, as the dog dies the moment he has seen his master again.
The hero of the poem enters his own hall disguised as the lowest of men, with the suitors unaware.
Comparing Ulysses to a rock conveys his unmoving endurance while he silently plans revenge.
The curse that Antinous die before marrying anticipates his death as the first suitor killed in the final battle.
Telemachus repeats his father's gesture, shaking his head in silence and brooding on revenge, linking father and son.
Hatred of Antinous is compared to the darkness of death, showing how deeply she loathes him.
Eumaeus compares the beggar's tale to the finest minstrel's song, stressing how spellbinding it was.
Telemachus' thunderous sneeze signals the suitors' coming doom.
Ulysses says he knows all about her husband, while the audience knows he is the husband.
